name: Benin Bronzes
info: The Benin Bronzes are several thousand brass and bronze plaques and sculptures made by Edo artists from the fourteenth century to decorate the royal palace of the Kingdom of Benin in what is now Edo State, Nigeria, and mostly taken by British forces in 1897.

facts.made: Edo artists of the Guild of Benin Bronze Casters, working under royal decree for the obas (kings) of the Kingdom of Benin, who monopolised bronze, ivory and gold
facts.form: Several thousand cast brass and bronze plaques, portrait heads, bells, jewellery and smaller pieces, made by lost-wax casting; the rectangular plaques are about 3.2 millimetres thick, and other pieces are of ivory, wood, ceramic, leather or cloth
facts.where: Largest holdings in the Ethnological Museum of Berlin and the British Museum in London, with other collections in Germany, France, the Netherlands, the United States and, third largest, in Nigerian museums, principally the Nigerian National Museum in Lagos
facts.known: the palace plaques called Ama; commemorative heads of obas and queen mothers; lost-wax casting; the leopard as the oba's emblem; the Benin Expedition of 1897; the long dispute over return to Nigeria

t: The Benin Bronzes decorated the palace of the obas of Benin and honoured the oba, the divine king, and the queen mother; only the king could own objects of bronze and ivory, and he could allow high-ranking people to use some of them.

Most of the plaques and other objects were taken by British forces during the Benin Expedition of 1897, and were then divided among museums and private collections in Britain, Germany, the United States and elsewhere.
Nigeria has asked for their return since independence in 1960, and from 2021 museums and governments began to transfer ownership, while the largest British collection stayed in London.
dyk: Late 19th-century scholars concluded that Benin metalworking came from Portuguese traders, a conclusion now held to be mistaken, since bronzes were made in Benin before the Portuguese arrived.
ev: By tradition, the son of the Oni of Ife taught Benin metal workers the art of casting bronze by the lost-wax technique
Edo artists began to produce the sculptures, some of which date to this century
Benin began to trade ivory, pepper and slaves with the Portuguese and used manillas bought from them as a metal source
The first of two golden ages of Benin metalwork is believed to have come in the reign of Oba Esigie
The second golden age is believed to have come in the reign of Oba Eresoyen, from 1735 to 1750
British forces sacked Benin City and took the works of art decorating the royal palace and the nobility's residences
The British Museum began to sell more than 30 Benin Bronzes to the Nigerian government, sales that stopped in 1972
Germany signed a political declaration to return 1,130 bronzes, and the Horniman Museum in London transferred its Benin Bronzes to Nigeria

sections.origins:
The Kingdom of Benin occupied southern parts of present-day Nigeria between the fourteenth and nineteenth centuries and was rich in sculptures of iron, bronze, wood, ivory and terracotta. The Benin Bronzes are several thousand metal plaques and sculptures that decorated the royal palace in Benin City, made by artists of the Edo people from the fourteenth century. Most of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and it is believed that two golden ages of Benin metalwork fell in the reigns of the obas Esigie (fl. 1550) and Eresoyen (1735–1750).

The Benin bronze tradition is thought to have derived from or been influenced by that of the older Kingdom of Ife in south-west Nigeria. Tradition holds that the son of the Oni, the sovereign of Ife, taught Benin metal workers lost-wax casting in the thirteenth century, and in 1939 heads very like Benin's were found at Ife, dated to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Late 19th-century scholars O. M. Dalton and Charles Hercules Read concluded that Benin metallurgy came from the Portuguese, an error, since bronzes were made in Benin before the Portuguese came.
sections.content:
The plaques, called Ama in the Edo language, depict scenes or themes from the history of the kingdom. They exist in two formats: one with turned-back vertical edges decorated with an incised guilloché pattern, and a narrower one without them. Most fronts are incised with foliate patterns of one to four leaves, called ebe-ame, the river leaf design; the leaves were used in healing rites by priestesses of Olokun, the god of the sea. Some reliefs show battles of the sixteenth-century wars of expansion, but most show dignitaries in ceremonial dress, usually static figures arranged around a central one. Many can be identified only by their clothing and emblems, which indicated rank and function, and attempts to link them with historical figures have been speculative and unverified.

The bronze heads were made for ancestral altars and held carved elephant tusks in openings in the top. Heads of the king or queen mother are archetypes, not individual portraits, and their style changed over the centuries. The leopard, which symbolises the oba, recurs in many pieces, as does the royal triad of the oba flanked by two assistants. Although called bronzes, most pieces are brass, an alloy of copper, zinc and lead in various proportions.
sections.making:
The palace was the site of production of the royal ancestral altars and of an elabourate court ceremonial life. Artists working in bronze were organised into a kind of guild under royal decree and lived in a special area of the palace under the oba's direct control. The oba monopolised the materials hardest to obtain, such as gold, elephant tusks and bronze. The figures were cast in relief by the lost-wax technique, with details incised in the wax model, and the plaques were hung on the palace pillars by nails punched through them. The quality of the work was higher when the king was especially powerful and could employ many specialists, and casters reached plaques only about 3 millimetres thick.

Benin began to trade ivory, pepper and slaves with the Portuguese in the late fifteenth century and used manillas, brass ingots in the form of bracelets bought from them, as a metal source. Their brass, once suggested to come from the Netherlands, is now thought to come from the Rhineland in Germany. According to some sources, Benin artists may have been inspired by items the Portuguese brought, but Babatunde Lawal cites relief carving in southern Nigeria to argue that the plaques are indigenous to Benin.
sections.reception:
As a courtly art, the objects aimed to glorify the oba and the history of his power, or to honour the Iyoba, the queen mother. When a king died, his successor ordered a bronze head of his predecessor, and installing an altar for the predecessor was a prerequisite for succession. In the annual festivals to reinforce the mystical power of the oba, the new king made offerings at these altars, held to be essential to the continuation of his reign. Approximately 170 of these heads survive, and their stylistic variation is the main scientific basis for a chronology.

Few African works had been collected by Europeans before the nineteenth century, and when more were taken to Europe they were described as curiosities of pagan cults. That attitude changed after 1897. The Benin Bronzes are more naturalistic than most African art of their period, and the lost-wax casting is considered among the best of African sculpture. A sixteenth-century bronze showing the Oba with Europeans featured in the BBC and British Museum series A History of the World in 100 Objects, begun in 2010. Ownership of bronze and ivory was reserved to the king, who could allow high-ranking individuals to use items such as hanging masks and cuffs.
sections.survival:
In January 1897 a party led by James Robert Phillips of the Niger Coast Protectorate set out toward Benin with six other British officials, two businessmen, translators and 215 porters. Its purpose is disputed: the stated aim was to negotiate with the oba, while some historians hold that it was a reconnaissance disguised as diplomacy, aimed at overthrowing him. The survivors said they were ambushed by the oba's warriors, and only two Europeans survived. A naval punitive expedition under Admiral Harry Rawson sacked and destroyed Benin City and took the works decorating the palace and the nobles' residences. The British account held that the attack answered an ambush of a peaceful mission and freed the population from a reign of terror. A 2020 book notes that since the 1960s historians have increasingly seen the expedition against Oba Ovonramwen as dictated by long-standing policy, not as retaliation.

Some pieces went to British officials, the Foreign Office sold many, mostly to German and American museums, and it gave a large number of plaques to the British Museum, which holds about 900 objects. By 1988, perhaps as few as fifty pieces remained in Nigeria while about 2,400 were in European and American collections. Dan Hicks gives a total of up to 10,000 looted objects.
sections.legacy:
Since independence in 1960 Nigeria has sought the return of the bronzes, a case regarded as a test of the debate over restitution of cultural objects from Africa, comparable to the Elgin Marbles. From 1950 to 1972 the British Museum sold more than 30 pieces to Nigeria as duplicates. In July 2022 Germany signed a declaration to return 1,130 bronzes, and a first 20 were handed over in Abuja that December. The Horniman Museum, the University of Aberdeen, Jesus College, Cambridge, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Smithsonian Institution also returned or transferred objects, and in 2025 the Netherlands returned 119. The British Museum's collection remains protected by an act of Parliament.

The returns have raised questions of ownership. In March 2023 President Muhammadu Buhari decreed that all repatriated objects belong to the Benin Royal Family, and Oba Ewuare II announced plans for a museum near his palace. Brigitta Hauser-Schäublin called Germany's 2022 restitution policy a fiasco. In 2022 the Restitution Study Group, an African-American reparations group, petitioned against returns, arguing that descendants of enslaved Africans should have co-ownership; the petition was denied. The Digital Benin database, launched in November 2022, lists over 5,000 artefacts held by more than 130 institutions in 20 countries.

summary: The Benin Bronzes are several thousand plaques and sculptures made by Edo artists from the fourteenth century for the palace of the obas of Benin. Most were taken by British forces in 1897 and scattered among museums, and since 2021 some have been returned to Nigeria.
references: Paddy Docherty, Blood and Bronze: The British Empire and the Sack of Benin (Hurst, 2021)
Dan Hicks, The Brutish Museums. The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution (Pluto Press, 2020)
Barnaby Phillips, LOOT: Britain and the Benin Bronzes (Oneworld Publications, 2022)
Frank Willett, African Art: An Introduction (Thames and Hudson, 1985)
